cards.h: Getting up is the hard part
cards.b: Reaching space is not about going high; it is about going sideways very fast. Everything in space travel, from satellites to Moon missions, follows from a few physics ideas: action and reaction, orbital speed and energy budgets.

Newton's third law: a rocket throws exhaust backward and is pushed forward. It needs no air, so it works in vacuum. Konstantin Tsiolkovsky wrote the rocket equation in 1903: the speed gained depends on exhaust speed and on the logarithm of the mass ratio, full to empty. Because fuel must lift fuel, most of a rocket is propellant, so we use stages, dropping empty tanks. Robert Goddard flew the first liquid-fuel rocket in 1926.

Newton imagined a cannon on a mountain: fire faster and the ball lands farther, until it falls around the curve of Earth and never lands. That is an orbit. Low Earth orbit needs about 7.8 km/s; at about 400 km the period is about 90 minutes. Astronauts float because they and the station are in free fall.

• Low Earth orbit (200 to 2,000 km): ISS, imaging.
  • Sun-synchronous: passes at the same local time, used for remote sensing.
  • Geostationary: 35,786 km above the equator, period 24 hours, appears fixed in the sky, used for communication (idea by Arthur C. Clarke, 1945).

Higher orbits move slower: Kepler's third law.

To leave Earth for good you need about 11.2 km/s (escape velocity). Missions rarely fly straight: a Hohmann transfer uses an elliptical path touching two orbits, the cheapest in fuel. Gravity assists let a probe steal a little of a planet's orbital energy; Voyager 2 used them to tour four planets.

Rockets used to be thrown away each time. Since the first booster landing in December 2015 (SpaceX Falcon 9), reusing boosters has cut launch costs sharply. Where space is the 'edge' is set by convention at the Karman line, 100 km up.

The German V-2 (1942) was the first rocket to reach space. After the war, Wernher von Braun and Sergei Korolev built the ones that launched the space age, from Sputnik in 1957. Orbital rules are verified every day by thousands of satellites whose paths follow Newton and Kepler.

• 'There is no gravity in orbit.' Gravity is about 90 percent as strong at the ISS; it is free fall that gives weightlessness.
  • 'Rockets push against air.' They push against their own exhaust.
  • 'Going up is the goal.' Sideways speed is the goal.

Tipu Sultan's Mysore army used iron-cased rockets against the British in the 1780s and 90s, an inspiration for Congreve's rockets. ISRO's story: Vikram Sarabhai founded INCOSPAR (1962); the first sounding rocket flew from Thumba on 21 November 1963; SLV-3 put Rohini into orbit in July 1980 under A.P.J. Abdul Kalam. PSLV (first launch 1993) became a workhorse; GSLV flew with the indigenous cryogenic engine in January 2014; LVM3 launched Chandrayaan-3.

• Rockets work by action and reaction; staging beats the rocket equation.
  • Orbit is free fall around Earth at about 7.8 km/s in low orbit.
  • Geostationary orbit is 35,786 km up with a 24 hour period.
  • Gravity assists and Hohmann transfers save fuel.

Think about it: (1) Why do rockets launch eastward when they can? (2) Why does a satellite in a higher orbit move slower?
